subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106, it is my honour and, indeed, a pleasure to present a petition on behalf of a number of western Canadians who indicate that the Conservative Government has really no mandate from the people of Canada to conclude a trade deal with the United States.
The petitioners believe that the proposed trade deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future; and would undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States. Since they also believe that the trade deal denies Canadians secure access to the United States market, which was the key objective of all of these negotiations, they are asking that Parliament dissolve now and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The Free Trade Agreement is a commercial accord between the world's two largest trading partners. It is not an environmental agreement. The environment was not, therefore, a subject for negotiation nor are environmental matters included in the text of the agreement. Our capability to deal with environmental issues at the national and international levels is unaffected by the FTA as our recently announced federal water policy makes clear. In the appropriate way and in the appropriate forums Canada will continue to pursue with vigour the objectives of its environmental policies.
On the broader question of international trade and the environment, the GATT has ruled that the environmental policies of a national government cannot be construed as an impediment to trade. Canada has long supported the GATT and will continue to do so.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-103, an Act to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada, to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and to make consequential and related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure and privilege to have the opportunity to speak in introducing this Bill at second reading. It is most appropriate that the House should resume its session today for the calendar year 1988 with this legislation which is designed to give a great upward boost and momentum to the cause of overcoming regional disparities in Atlantic Canada.
The Bill was introduced just before Christmas. It was forecast in the Speech from the Throne, and I will refer to that in a few moments. I might point out that it was in 1969 that the former Department of Regional Economic Expansion was established and over the past 20 or 25 years we have seen a variety of programs and expenditures aimed at reducing regional disparities in Canada.
I think it must be said that the Government that was here before us and previous Governments over the last 20 or 25 years have endorsed the principles of overcoming regional disparity and of trying to develop all regions of Canada. In fact, I do not know of any other nation in the world where so much emphasis is put on regional development and on attempting to overcome regional disparities.
In any event, the old DREE was established in 1969. In the early 1970s, there were the beginnings of general development agreements with subagreements for specific purposes. Spending was shared between the federal and provincial Governments, the higher proportion coming from the Government of Canada. Two of the principal industrial incentive programs of the Government of Canada have been the Regional Development Incentives Act and under that Act the Industrial and Regional Development Program.
It should be pointed out, to put it in the proper context, that federal regional development spending under GDAs, ERDAs and under the RDIA and IRDP programs did slacken off, I think would perhaps be the right term, over recent years until

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
1984-85. For example, there was very little growth in federal government spending in the Atlantic provinces on these major development programs in 1984-85 as compared to 1976-77. In 1984-85, spending under those programs in the Atlantic region was only 10 per cent higher than it was in 1976-77 while spending in Canada as a whole was 77 per cent higher.
The early 1980s was a period of retrenchment on the part of the Government of Canada and that is shown by the fact that spending in the Atlantic region for those programs in 1981-82 was only 3 per cent higher than it was in 1976-77 despite the inflation that had occurred in the intervening period. In addition, the proportion of the Canadian total going to the Atlantic region had declined dramatically during that period.
There has been some improvement in spending under these programs in Atlantic Canada from 1984-85 to the present time, but quite clearly, apart all together from the need for increased spending, it is quite clear that there is a need for changes in approach as well. That is what the present legislation is designed to do.
We all know, at least those of us who are objective, rational and honest in our approach, that there has been considerable improvement in the economic environment in Atlantic Canada under the administration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney). Some 1,118,000 jobs were created under this Government's policies in effect since September, 1984. In relative terms, jobs have been created in Canada at a faster rate than in any other major OECD nation. Of those, 81,000 were created in Atlantic Canada. That is some improvement but not nearly enough. It is a very considerable improvement, of course, over the record of our Liberal predecessors.
Employment has risen and the unemployment rate has fallen in every Atlantic province, indeed in every province, during this period. In Atlantic Canada total unemployment fell by 30,000 from September, 1984, to the present, compared to an increase of 68,000 under the last Liberal Government of former Prime Minister Trudeau. That is a significant improvement but of course not enough. In September of 1984, when the Mulroney Government took office, unemployment in Atlantic Canada was 17 per cent. By October of 1987, just over three years later, it had fallen to 13.2 per cent; still a significant figure but a decrease of almost 4 per cent.
The number of Atlantic Canada families living below the poverty line decreased during the same period from 16.4 per cent in 1984 to 15.8 per cent in 1986; a small decrease, but nevertheless a decrease. The number of single people in Atlantic Canada living below the poverty line decreased by almost 10 per cent, from 48 per cent in 1984 to 38.6 per cent in 1986. The free trade agreement will of course further reduce the number of Atlantic Canadians living below the poverty line because it will increase the number of jobs, increase real incomes, and reduce consumer prices. This is particularly appropriate for Atlantic Canada because it has for 100 years
been seeking ways to improve the terms of trade with our partners to the south. The region is achieving that at last under the leadership of the Prime Minister.
As I said, there has been a considerable improvement in the economic environment in Atlantic Canada since the last election, but of course this is not enough. We are not satisfied with it. The Prime Minister is not satisfied with it. Our Atlantic Ministers are not satisfied with it. It has not been enough and more needs to be done. That is why the present legislation is before us.
On October 1, 1986, in the Speech from the Throne, the Government promised a bold new approach to regional development. That is encompassed in this Bill. The Speech from the Throne said this:
It is time to consider new approaches, to examine how' our considerable and growing support for Canada's regions can be used more efficiently, more effectively and with greater sensitivity to local conditions and opportunities.
That is one of the main features of the approach in this legislation, greater sensitivity to local conditions and opportunities. It went on to say that we are convinced:
- many positive proposals for new policy initiatives will come from those who live and work in the regions concerned.
That is a central principle of this legislation. The speech went on to say:
As a first step in achieving improved results from this sustained national approach, an Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be constituted to facilitate and co-ordinate all federal development initiatives in the area. This agency will make full use of the expertise available in the Atlantic region and invite the maximum participation of other Governments and organizations in the area.
That is what the Speech from the Throne in 1986 said and that is what the legislation now before the House does. Mr. McPhail and Senator Murray have put in place the machinery to carry out these pledges in a Speech from the Throne which was one of the most momentous in Canadian history to date. Under it, a whole series of very important policies have been adopted and implemented by the Government, including the free trade agreement, the Meech Lake constitutional Accord, the new approach to defence, child care, and other policies of which we will hear a great deal during the next few months.
The Prime Minister promised to consult with Atlantic Canadians in establishing the new regional development agency promised in the Speech from the Throne. The result is the ACOA which will be operated by and for Atlantic Canadians. It has been devised by Atlantic Canadians. It has not been imposed upon them from someone here in Ottawa, such as a former mayor now in this House or someone who doubtless believes that they understand everything that happens in Canada because they happen to live in the national capital and scoot off somewhere in the region of Ontario to get elected to this Parliament and tell us how the world works outside Ottawa. They of course think that the world is Ottawa. There is a great world out there that is not Ottawa or Ontario. The result, of course, of our approach, which is different-

The Prime Minister, and certainly we Atlantic Ministers, were not satisfied with an increase in spending of 35 per cent. That is why we have committed an additional $1.05 billion over the next five years. We have already increased the spending that existed when the Liberals were in office in 1984-85 by 35 per cent. We are not satisfied with a 10 per cent, 20 per cent or 35 per cent increase. We have stated that we will continue spending on these programs or similar programs and will add to that level another $1.05 billion over the next five years. Our commitment is for an additional $200 million yearly for five years, which is an increase of twice the spending in this Government's effort to overcome regional disparity in Atlantic Canada. My hon. friends opposite may have some criticism, but I know they will support this program.
Let me refer to the Bill. The purpose is stated in Clause 4, which is:
To increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada and,
more particularly, to enhance the growth of earned incomes and employment
opportunities in that region.
That is what we want for the region. We want an increase in earned income, not a transfer in income.
The object of the Bill is described in Clause 12, which states:
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
The object of the Agency is to support and promote opportunity for economic development of Atlantic Canada, with particular emphasis on small and medium-sized enterprises, through policy, program and project development and implementation and through advocacy of the interests of Atlantic Canada in national economic policy, program and project development and implementation.
Clause 4 and Clause 12 describe the purpose and object of the Bill, with particular emphasis on small and medium-sized enterprises. That is the purpose of the agency, not to spend $1 billion on general infrastructure in Atlantic Canada. This money will not be used for those purposes, which are the purposes of the present regional development spending under current ERDA and other agreements.
This money will not be used for the sewerage out of Halifax Harbour or Saint John's Harbour. That is not its purpose.

That is its purpose, not to pave streets, build roads and so on, as will continue to be done under ERDA type agreements.
In addition, the agency will have an advocacy role. It will be empowered to formulate plans to support economic development in Atlantic Canada in consort with all other federal departments. No federal department will be able to operate in Atlantic Canada without input from this agency. The agency will ensure that any initiative of the federal Government in Atlantic Canada is harnessed to the goal of increasing opportunities for economic development in Atlantic Canada.
As one person said, it is like having a friend fighting for us in Ottawa. In addition to Atlantic Canada Members and Atlantic Canada Ministers, this agency will have the object of fighting for Atlantic Canadians in Ottawa. This never happened before.

Canada. This provision is contained in Clause 5(2) of the legislation.
Clause 9 provides for another unprecedented power. It gives the Minister the unique authority to transfer, conditionally or unconditionally, funds from ACOA to supplement the funds of another Minister for a project that the Minister of ACOA is satisfied will further the objectives of this legislation. If another minister has a project that is very helpful to Atlantic Canada, the Minister responsible for ACOA can decide to supplement the funding there. He will have the right under Clause 7 to designate areas within Atlantic Canada for specific periods of time. He will select those areas because they provide exceptional opportunities for economic development. This gives the Minister real flexibility so that he can designate as such, * an area that has an exceptional opportunity for economic development. That is in addition to his present authority to create special areas under the special areas legislation. If the Minister must create a designated area or a special area in Atlantic Canada, he can do so.
Clause 8 provides another new power. It gives the Minister the right to acquire stock options and to exercise rights under those options in connection with any loan guarantee, or credit insurance, grant or contribution.
The Minister is also empowered to enter into federal-provincial agreements with the provinces of Atlantic Canada subject to approval by the Governor in Council. In that respect he will have the same powers the Minister of DRIE had with respect to ERDA subsidiary agreements.
This is another illustration of the Prime Minister's policy of building a stronger Canada based on co-operative federal-provincial relations. This is not talking about co-operative federalism, as did the last Government under former Prime Minister Trudeau, and then imposing the iron-shod heel on the provinces. No, this is not talking abut co-operative federalism on the one hand and doing the exact opposite on the other hand, what I used to call "jackboot" democracy. Do Hon. Members remember when we had jackboot democracy in this country? My God, if one disagreed with the Liberal administration it put the boots right to you, jack and all. Well, we do not have that any longer. We have co-operative federal-provincial relations.
This will enable federal and provincial governments to work together on priority initiatives to give opportunities for economic development. Its success will in part depend on the provincial governments and their co-operation as well. The Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) will remember that sometimes it is not all that easy to get co-operation from provincial governments. Perhaps he will enlighten us on that when he speaks.

It is interesting to see the successful turn in Cape Breton and the atmosphere of greater hope and greater positive prospects. It has taken over the processes for applications under existing regional development programs such as the Atlantic Enterprise Program. These processes are now being greatly streamlined. You will not believe this, Mr. Speaker, because you are used to how things were done in the past under the former Liberal administration and how much time it took, but 90 per cent of all applications can now be processed at the provincial ACOA offices. Ninety per cent of Atlantic Enterprise Program applications, for example, can be dealt with by Gordon Slade and his people at the office in St. John's or at the offices in Charlottetown, Halifax or Moncton. The facts are straightforward. Over the three years that the Government has been in power regional development spending has decreased by over 30 per cent. Regional development spending has decreased by $3 billion in the three years that the Government has been in power. That is the reality.
What does that leave us? It leaves us with a Government, in the face of an ever shrinking commitment to regional development spending, inventing new names and giving higher local profiles to new agencies in an attempt to give a greater emphasis to a shrinking commitment and a shrinking regional development dollar in Atlantic Canada to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. In western Canada there is a Western Initiatives Program. Both these programs are designed to cover up, to camouflage, the fact that the Government has reduced both in spirit and in financial terms its commitment to combat regional disparity and to seek as a target some minimal level of services no matter where one lives.
The Minister of Transport, who is a former Minister of Justice, a year or a year and a half ago stood in the House to say that he wanted to bring in a Bill, if he could obtain the consent of the provinces, to do away with the Senate, that unelected chamber that has no role in a modern democracy. I found it passing strange to see that self-same former Minister of Justice stand in his place today as the Minister of Transport acting as an apologist for the real power and the real Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Senator Lowell Murray. This same Minister who wanted to abolish the Senate because it was fundamentally undemocratic and fundamentally non-representative has now been relegated to the role of a mouthpiece and an apologist for the Senator who has the real power, to the extent that there is any, for development in Atlantic Canada.
Canadians should be asking themselves why it is that of the 17 to 20 Members elected from Atlantic Canada and the half a dozen Ministers elected from Atlantic Canada in the Conservative Party, not one of those Members of Parliament enjoys enough of the Prime Minister's confidence to be named the Minister responsible for the Atlantic Opportunities Agency. Having reviewed the resumes of every single Conservative Member from Atlantic Canada, starting with the
January 18, 1988

Minister of Transport, why did the Prime Minister of Canada find it necessary to go to the Senate and pick a Senator to be the Minister responsible for running the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency? Is it because the Minister of Transport and his colleagues in the Cabinet from Atlantic Canada lack the confidence, the bravado, and the desire to pilot this agency through with legislation and into new programs, or was it because he wanted to put the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency out of the reach of parliamentarians and off into another chamber because this agency is so good, dynamic, and fantastic and it will make such a difference to Atlantic Canada that the Prime Minister in his wisdom did not want it to have a chance to be show-cased in the House of Commons?
It is an extreme contradiction in terms. On the one hand there is this view expressed by the Minister of Transport, the mouthpiece for Senator Lowell Murray, that this is a great upward boost

I call it the "great upward goose"-something the Government wants to brag about. But on the other hand the authority for the agency is vested not in the House of Commons, not with an elected Member from Atlantic Canada, but with a Senator in the other place named for another region of this country. That very fact alone should have people in Atlantic Canada wondering about the new Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
This agency was first announced in the Speech from the Throne in October of 1986, a year and a half ago. It was subsequently reannounced during the by-election which sent my friend from St. John's East to Parliament, with all of the accompanying extravaganza. We did not receive the first inkling of a piece of legislation for this new agency until the very last day the House sat before the Christmas break. That is the high profile and the importance that the Government attaches to this new agency. A year and a half after he announced it, the Minister, on behalf of his boss, Senator Murray, has finally stated in the House that he would like to introduce legislation.
What happened in the intervening 18 months? I hold in my hand a thick sheaf of press releases issued by the Minister of Transport's boss, Senator Lowell Murray, on behalf of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Every one of them begins with the words, "Senator Lowell Murray", or in some cases, "the Minister of Transport on behalf of Senator Lowell Murray," announced today such and such a program. There are all kinds of them. This Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency has obviously been busy.
When one goes through the announcements, one discovers that every single program announced has funding that comes out of existing federal government programs and existing grants that have nothing to do with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Lo and behold, when ACOA is examined under a microscope, rather than from the dramatic distance of the Minister of Transport's words, it is discovered that not one single penny, not a red cent, has been spent by the
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency since its announcement 18 months ago, and since its official kick-off in June of last year by the Prime Minister in the middle of a by-election in St. John's, Newfoundland.
Not one penny has been expended. Yet today we hear the Minister of Transport telling us that we ought to be pleased because, unlike previous programs, 90 per cent of the applications can be rapidly expedited, faster than was ever done before. The Minister of Transport knows that not one single application has been expedited, and not one single penny has been spent by the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency since it was announced 18 months ago. Let us get the facts straight before we allow the Minister of Transport to get carried away with his message, perhaps to carry away some of the people of Atlantic Canada as well.
The true measure of how autonomous, relevant, and independent minded this new board will be that runs the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is perhaps best measured by what has happened in the City of Moncton. In the City of Moncton the closure of the CN Shops has already cost some 850 jobs. Those jobs are permanently lost. This is in the self-same city that is the headquarters for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
How did the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the appropriate Ministers respond to this great loss of jobs in the City of Moncton? 1 can tell you how they did not respond, Mr. Speaker. A few days ago CN put out another press release announcing that the remaining 350 employees at the CN yards in Moncton will be receiving notices of their jobs being lost in the near future. I am told that as of September 30 the CN Shops will be closed. The answer to the first 850 jobs being lost is to wipe out 350 more. That is right in the backyard of the headquarters of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. This latest announcement and death blow for Moncton comes despite the fact that the Minister of Transport and his predecessor, the gentleman who is currently the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mazankowski), both assured the people of Moncton that the Government of Canada was going to find a solution to the dramatic loss of jobs in the City of Moncton. Neither the Minister's predecessor nor the Minister have delivered on the solemn commitment given in the House, repeatedly and in particular in answer to questions from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud).
There will be a board of 16 or 18 members. If one listened carefully, at least to the names read out and put on the public record by the Minister of Transport of board members from Newfoundland, three of whom are well known Conservative fund raisers and Party supporters, and in the last month one of whom had a front page expose on his Tory Party connections and was proud to talk about them in the Sunday Express. When I listened to those three or four names of prominent, hard core Conservative fund raisers, and if I assumed from that list of names that in the other Atlantic Provinces people were drawn for similar reasons, then one has to ask-and this

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
is very important-to what extent will this board be an independent semi-autonomous agency that functions independent of thought and action of the governing Party of the day?
How can Atlantic Canadians be issued the challenge of the Minister of Transport that "Ottawa cannot solve your problems, you must solve your own problems; you come with the solutions and we may or may not come with the money", when the board that has been set up to expedite that process is made up of intimate friends of the Party in power today and Conservative fund raisers? How can anyone be expected to believe that this board will operate independently, notwithstanding the views of the Minister of Transport and his colleagues from Atlantic Canada, and notwithstanding the views of the boss of the Minister of Transport, Senator Lowell Murray?
It seems to me that, as I stated, we have been given the golden goose, not a golden boost. It does not lay golden eggs. On the one hand we have been told to solve our own problems, and on the other hand our so-called independent voice has been stacked with friends of the Government who will take their instructions from the Government. That is the reality; there is no independent voice.
Why is that important and such a major point in this debate today? I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. Over the last two or three years, and I humbly submit particularly in Atlantic Canada, there has grown a degree of cynicism about the so-called objective means through which individuals and businesses receive grants from government, the likes of which we have never seen. There has been a proliferation of new lobby companies, a proliferation of people who will represent you to the Government and you pay if you get what you ask for. One of the better known companies is GCI, Government Consultants International and this week's Report On Business Magazine has a huge article on it. The company is headed up by former Conservative Premier Frank Moores.
Why is it important that all of the board members on ACOA are Conservatives? The article points out that this new lobby company, set up by former Conservative Frank Moores of Newfoundland, a good colleague and friend of the Minister of Transport, has established a new system to lobby on behalf of clients. It is called a pay if you win system. If you are looking for a fishing license you hire GCI, give it a flat retainer-or lobster licences in recent days-of $25,000 and if, miraculously, you get your licence-I am told there is a pretty good batting average-you continue to pay $5,000 a month for three years. This is all outlined in the Report on Business Magazine.
On the one hand we have an agency with a so-called billion dollars in new funds. It is not new funds and I will come to that. We have a so-called independent board made up of the most blue-backed dyed-in-the wool Conservatives the Government could find and we have a new system in place in Ottawa,
a new ethic, pay if you win, pay as you go and hire GCI former Conservative Premier Frank Moores and Mr. Doucet, another well known name around these places. That is the new Ottawa, Mr. Speaker.
So what do we have here? GCI is acting for Petro-Canada, a Crown corporation. GCI is acting for Canadian National, another Crown corporation. Is GCI acting for ACOA? This is the same GCI which charged Mr. Snarby $2,000 for a licence plus a $500 a month retainer after he was turned down by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) and by all of the bureaucrats in Ottawa. Having been turned down, and on appeal at every level rejected again, miraculously Mr. Snarby got a licence that formerly he could not get. Is that the way ACOA is going to do business?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What about Francis Fox?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Or Mr. Fox. It does not matter. This kind of lobbying is unacceptable and this kind of development in Ottawa under the Government is unacceptable to all the people of Canada no matter who is employed and who is involved. You can name whatever names you want.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: You are not too convincing.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
This is the same company that just recently helped a Nova Scotia company get lobster licences. It was on the national news, rejected by the Premier of Nova Scotia, the Minister of Fisheries of Nova Scotia, the opposition leaders of Nova Scotia and the fishermen of Nova Scotia. This is the same company that helped the same Halifax company get a licence. GCI took on the assignment for an initial fee of $10,000 but told the client that if it got the licence it would have to cough up an additional $25,000 a year for four years. GCI denied that and said it was charging $25,000 a year for three years, not four years. It said "We have been misrepresented". So a public relations firm for a fee of $85,000 arranges lobster licences for a so-called free market-some free market-and a free enterprise firm-some free enterprise firm-in Nova Scotia.
This so-called billion dollar agency is established with a board of directors no more independent of the Minister of Transport than the Minister who tags along at his side. The board of directors is made up of appointments not named by agencies and groups in the region. The Atlantic Chamber of Commerce was not asked to name somebody; nor was the Development Association Movement of Newfoundland and nor were the various agencies for development in Atlantic Canada. The Government polled to find out who were the staunchest Tories in the land and named them to the board. The Government is telling us that the board is to be autonomous.
As I said, in the Prime Minister's Ottawa, we are paying for contracts and licences as a way of life. Frankly, it terrifies me that that kind of board has been named which will have access to such amounts of money, and responding to the wishes of the
January 18, 1988

Minister of Transport or his boss in the Senate, Senator Murray. They are part of an administration in which paying for access and paying for the right decisions has become commonplace. It should never be commonplace.
The Minister of Transport in announcing this Bill today talks about decentralization as if it were a wonderful new thing. The Minister knows that in 1982 a system of federal development co-ordinators was established in Atlantic Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The Minister is leaving.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
He has to go to his press conference to launch another, no doubt, great initiative.
Federal development co-ordinators were named in 1982. Each of these co-ordinators were tasked with the responsibility of co-ordinating the efforts of all federal line departments in each of the provinces. There was one for each of the Atlantic provinces. That led to a much decentralized decision-making process.
ACOA is expanding that process. One could almost argue that it is moving away from decentralization to some extent because now there is a head office in Moncton whereas before each province had a federal development co-ordinator officer who reported directly to Ottawa. One did not have to go through Moncton or any other regional office, but directly to the Minister in Ottawa. We have the same system except now we have another layer of bureaucracy so that there is no direct line of communication between New Brunswick's federal coordinating officer and Ottawa. New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, P.E.I. and Newfoundland must all go through the Atlantic regional office. 1 do not know whether one can call that further decentralization. I suspect in reality it may to some extent be the opposite.
The Government says there will be a billion dollars or a little more than a billion dollars in funding over five years, $200 million a year for the entire Atlantic region. If you break it down that way it does not sound as intimidating, but there are many of us who question this notion that it is new funding over five years. I noted earlier today during the Minister's speech, and he did not disagree, that 1RDP will be phased out in June of this year. I do not need to tell you, Mr. Speaker, because of your extreme sensitivity and great awareness of all the regions of Canada the importance of IRDP and the role it has played in Atlantic Canada and elsewhere in the country. That program which the Minister said is being transferred to ACOA will be phased out in June. As part of the reorganization of DRIE, no doubt other programs-this one has been confirmed-are on the block to be phased out.
How can the Government in good conscience on the one hand claim in excess of $1 billion in new money, moneys over and above what would have been spent in any case, when in the next breath the Minister in this House admits that IRDP, among others-is being phased out. There is no indication yet where the moneys that would have been spent under IRDP are going or whether there will be a replacement program.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
What is occurring is a consolidation of the DRIE, a consolidation of existing programs and elimination of some of those programs, and as those programs are eliminated the funds will be used to pay for new programs under ACOA. It is not new money; it is not a new initiative. It is certainly not $1 billion in new money.
The Minister chose during the course of his remarks to talk about free trade and regional development. The Minister will know that in the weeks leading up to the issuing of the final text of the free trade agreement, I and many other members of my Party, in the House and elsewhere, have categorically, repeatedly, day after day put the question to the Prime Minister. We asked him if there would be language in the final text which would specifically exempt regional development programs from U.S. trade law. That question, clearly, simply and without preamble, was put repeatedly to the Prime Minister of Canada.
While a direct answer to that question was very carefully never given, as I know from reviewing the transcripts, the Prime Minister or whoever else was answering in his absence always left the impression that there was nothing to be concerned about, that regional development would be covered and not to worry about it. 1 challenge any Hon. Member of the House to read the final text of the free trade agreement and to show me where there is a written exemption from U.S. trade law for regional development programs, because no such wording or exemption exists.
In the face of the lack of an exemption and of previous rulings made by the U.S. Commerce Department, Atlantic Canadians are correct to be concerned about free trade and regional development. That is why the Atlantic Provinces Chamber of Commerce, during committee hearings in Atlantic Canada, refused to endorse free trade. It refused to endorse it because of the uncertainty that existed at that stage over whether or not an exemption would exist.
I invite Hon. Members to read the softwood lumber ruling of last year made by the U.S. Department of Commerce. They will find within that ruling made by the U.S. Department of Commerce an almost categorical and complete list of all the regional development programs in this country that are countervailable and subject to U.S. trade law. We all know that one of the clauses in the free trade agreement provides that all existing rulings made by the Department of Commerce or the U.S. courts on trade action stand.
Given that the softwood lumber decision stands, given that almost all of our regional development programs are listed as being countervailable, and given that there is no exemption for regional development programs in the final text, how can the Minister of Transport rise in his place and tell us today that we ought not be concerned about the future of regional development programs?

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
That brings me to my last point. We are told, though it is difficult to know, that the Government has designed the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency to respond to the private sector, period. There is nothing wrong with designing a program to respond to the private sector, providing that there are complementary programs to continue the work of building up the infrastructure and the public sector at the same time.
To clear away the smoke and mirrors so that the people may understand what is happening, basically what is happening is that the Government of Canada has said that it is out of the business of infrastructure in Atlantic Canada. It is no longer interested in that. Whether it is highways, wharves and harbour development, water and sewer, educational facilities, post-secondary and primary or otherwise, or any of those kinds of programs or infrastructures, the basic underpinnings of the ability of any region to be competitive, the Government of Canada is out of the business. The Government will tailor this program and these funds primarily to respond to the private sector, period.
If a person lives in a part of Atlantic Canada in which the basic infrastructure is not up to national standards and is looking to ACOA to solve the problem or to assist in that problem, forget it. If a person lives in Halifax, Moncton, Saint John, St. John's or Charlottetown where there is basic industrial infrastructure in place, then that person can apply. It might be wise for that person to call GCI so that it would represent him, but he can apply. However, those who live in parts of Atlantic Canada which do not even have basic decent highway systems, where every summer the choice is between running the fish plant or having a bath at night because there is not enough water for both, where the school system is dilapidated and falling down around their ears, and there are far too many places like that in Atlantic Canada, then ACOA is not for them. It is not their agency. ACOA is a closed door.
No conscientious Member from Atlantic Canada, recognizing that continued reality of Atlantic Canada, a reality of which we are not proud and not happy, can accept that this is the primary development initiative of the Government of Canada. We cannot accept that the philosophy that those who have nothing will get nothing and those who have infrastructure may hire GCI and might get a grant is the philosophy of winners and losers, and that those who happen to be the losers in a losing region are told: "Tough luck, buddy, move to Toronto". No, I cannot accept that kind of philosophy.
When DREE was established in 1969, exactly the opposite prevailed as the raison d'etre for establishing a department focused entirely on regional development. The philosophy was not that we ought to pour money into the region for a 10-week cycle but that we ought to recognize that before we can cultivate and build an entrepreneurial spirit in the private sector we must first put in place the underpinnings, the infrastructure necessary to be on an equal footing and to be competitive in the Canadian or the Atlantic market-place.
A lot of progress was made. The Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) and I represent a part of Newfoundland where only in the last 10 to 15 years, and really only in the last five or six years, a highway covering an area of 500 miles of coastline has been completed. Just 15 or 20 years ago the highway was a cow path. The best bet to get up the coast was by boat. There has not been a paved road up the northern peninsula for all that long. We are just now in the process-

speechtext: Only since the PC Government got in.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity- Conception (Mr. Johnson) knows what I am saying. The road was finished before the PC Government got elected.
What are the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador and I doing now? We are now trying to get basic infrastructure like water and sewer into these communities to allow industrial and secondary development in the fishery. However, the ACOA program is not interested in that kind of development.
We endorse the basic principle of more autonomy and more decisions being taken in the region. However, we only endorse it when it is real, when the board has a mandate to be autonomous and not merely an echo sounding-board for Tory thought in Ottawa. We endorse the principle of targeting a region to try to come to grips with regional development programs, but not when the Government walks away from the responsibility, objectives and aims of developing the infrastructure of the region.
We look forward to seeing this Bill brought to committee. Indeed, we look forward to giving the many agencies and groups in Atlantic Canada which are not represented on this board and were not even invited to participate on it an opportunity to have their say about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Before this process is finished, we shall be proposing amendments to ensure that this agency, if it is to be established, functions as an agency that works on behalf of the people of Atlantic Canada on the initiative of Atlantic Canada and not as an agency that functions as a pre-election ploy on the part of the Conservative Government of Canada which finds itself in desperate need of raising its profile in the Atlantic region.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) speaking on behalf of the Senate on this issue. I have also listened with great interest to my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), speaking on the same issue. I am pleased to have an opportunity to put to the House my views on what is probably the most important economic issue for Canada from now until the end of this century; that is, the issue of regional development. That is not just my view or that of my Party, it is also the view expressed by the Economic Council of Canada in its report released September 30, 1987. That Council looked at the next
January 18, 1988

five years and said that the national economy is likely to expand steadily in coming years but uneven regional growth will be the country's major economic problem.
In dealing with that issue we do not require a Government response which is either a hoax or an attempt to baffle and confuse the people of Canada, particularly Atlantic Canada, into thinking it has done something where others have failed. I will repeat the figures quoted by the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe with respect to the Government's reduction in the amount of money spent on regional development in Atlantic Canada. Over the last three years it amounted to a reduction of $1 billion per year. The Government has replaced that with what it calls $1 billion, but it is actually $200 million a year. That tells the people of Canada how important the Government thinks the most serious economic problem in Canada is. The former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion was criticized for cutting $3 billion from regional development funding since 1984. It was also pointed out that the share of regional development dollars did not flow to the east or to the west as one might expect, but into central Canada.
The Minister of Transport quoted from the Throne Speech. That speech also said that spending more money by itself has not solved the problem. How hypocritical can the Government get? It takes $3 billion from regional development funding and then lectures Canadians on how spending money by itself will not solve the problem. I can tell you for sure that removing $3 billion from regional development will certainly not solve the problem. Giving back $200 million a year over five years is not going to solve the problem.
Since Confederation, 1 suppose, we have had certain regional disparities. Given the elaborate attention paid to the idea of regional development by previous Governments we would expect to see these disparities narrow. Yet that has not happened. In fact, the disparity in the unemployment rate between Ontario, where it is the lowest in the country, and the Atlantic provinces has increased over the last five years, not decreased. Relatively speaking, Atlantic Canadians are worse off now than they were five, six or seven years ago. That is not progress. In fact, it underscores exactly what the Economic Council of Canada has said, that regional disparity is the most serious economic problem we face.
It is not merely an economic problem either. It affects individuals and communities all across Atlantic Canada. People have to face the prospect of unemployment and the loss of dignity associated with the inability to contribute to the economy and their own lives. Youth unemployment is extremely serious. The ability of women to participate in the labour force has been diminished.
The Minister of Transport tried to brag about the past three years of Conservative Government, particularly with respect to Atlantic Canada. Yet Atlantic Canada fared very badly with
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
respect to regional development. During the first 18 months of Conservative Government the expenditure in Newfoundland, which has the highest unemployment rate in the country, was 1 per cent of the dollars available for regional development. If unemployment and other economic problems were spread evenly across the country on the basis of population we would have expected to get at least 2 per cent. Yet, no, under a Conservative Government Newfoundland received 1 per cent.
During that period of Tory administration, we have seen a reduction of regional development spending and a distortion of the spending in favour of central Canada at the expense of the region that needed it most, Atlantic Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Where was Crosbie?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Where was the Minister of Transport then? Where was Senator Murray then? Where were the other Ministers and Members from Newfoundland and the other Atlantic provinces when this was going on?
Even during the five-year period from 1981 to 1985 Newfoundland received on average 4.5 per cent of federal regional development dollars, or four and a half times the amount it received in the first 18 months of the Tory Government. Therefore I ask the House to reflect on what the Minister has said, given those astounding figures.
The Government has decreased regional development funding by $3 billion from 1984 to the present and yet it pretends that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is going to provide us with an answer to development in Atlantic Canada. The Government takes away $1 billion and gives back $200 million. That amounts to 20 cents on the dollar and it appears to be all we can expect. It is a hoax, a sleight of hand that the Government is trying to perpetrate on the Canadian people.
It has been suggested that what is happening is a decentralization of decision-making in all of Atlantic Canada. That is another hoax. Not only that, it is a derogation of the responsibility of the federal Government which is trying to get rid of the responsibility for regional development. We have heard the Minister of Transport say today that Atlantic Canadians are responsible for their own destiny, just as the poor are responsible for their poverty. The approach is to blame Atlantic Canadians; it is their fault, and they have to solve the problem. We have had enough of it.
One of those famous Atlantic Ministers who is going to be responsible for ACOA calls it the last kick at the can. The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be the last kick at the can as far as development programs for this region are concerned. In March of last year the former Public Works Minister stated that they had tried just about everything in the Atlantic region. They are now throwing up their hands. Two hundred million dollars a year will be the last kick at the can for Atlantic Canadians.

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
The Minister of Transport has said that setting up a board and allowing decisions to be made in Atlantic Canada is the last kick at the can, and they will wait four or five years to see if it works. The people of Atlantic Canada will not wait four or five years to have a hoax foisted upon them by the Government. The people of Atlantic Canada cannot afford to wait four or five years to have the Government of Canada look after their most serious problems.
The Minister of Transport says that decentralization is taking place and decisions will be made in Atlantic Canada. However that is not what the Senator said. In June, 1987, he said that the decisions will be made by him here in Ottawa. That is what Senator Murray said when asked where decentralized decision-making will take place. The final decisions will be made here in Ottawa by the Senator and if we have any questions about them we will ask the Minister of Transport to ask the Senator what he has to say about them.
The Government will take away $1 billion a year and put back $200 million, 20 cents on the dollars. The Government is telling Atlantic Canadians that it is now up to them to make a success of it. The Government will give them 20-cent dollars to work with and will put the responsibility on them. If this fails after four or five years the Government will blame Atlantic Canadians. It has absolved itself of responsibility for regional development.
The Government has set up a board of cronies and appointees with a few government people from the various provinces. 1 understand that this board represents the regional decisionmaking. However, in the legislation itself the board has no power, no decision-making authority. It is estalished by Section 18 of the Act. It is to be appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister. The object of the board is to assist the agency in the exercise of its powers and in the performance of its duties and functions. It is only to assist the agency. It has no decision-making power and no authority. Nowhere throughout the rest of the Act is there any mention of what role the board will play. It exists and can be called together from time to time by the president who operates under the direction of the Minister.
The Minister has already said that the decisions will be made by him in Ottawa. That is another part of the sham that the Government is trying to foist upon the people of Atlantic Canada. The Government has put all the Atlantic Canada regional development programs under one department, which is a good thing. At least there is a focus for Atlantic Canada in this legislation.
There will be input from business people, a very narrow sector of the Atlantic economy, but there are no representatives from a very substantial part of the Atlantic Canada enterprise, the co-operative sector. There are no representatives from the very substantial regional development councils,
associations, and corporations which exist in Atlantic Canada. These people are concerned about development in their parts of the country, but there is no representation by them. We have only business people, insurance executives, fundraisers for the Tory Party, and one person at least from each of the provinces who appears to be a representative of a government secretariat. There will be some input from Atlantic Canada but the decision-making has not changed substantially. We are not receiving any new thrust or effort through this legislation.
In the history of regional disparity there has been no improvement in Atlantic Canada. Elizabeth Beale is an economist and specialist analysing the Atlantic regional problems and related policy. She is the chief economist of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. She has reported that there has been very little improvement in any of the major indicators of regional disparity between the Atlantic provinces and the country as a whole since the 1960s. subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-SUGGESTED PRESENTATION TO UNITED STATES OF BILL FOR DAMAGES
speechtext:
Mr, Speaker, last week Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) met with his U.S, counterpart to discuss common issues. We are told that in that conversation the Secretary of State raised the question of acid rain and pretended that there is hope in obtaining cuts in the U.S. pollution coming into Canada.
Has the Secretary of State for External Affairs forgotten that because of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) decision to endorse the five-year U.S. clean coal technology program, the U.S. administration does not have to listen to Canada? Canada is now stuck with that endorsement and the Secretary of State knows it. Clearly the Government goofed.
If the Secretary of State really wants to obtain acid gas pollution cuts in the United States, he would assemble the costs and prepare a bill for damages to be presented by the Prime Minister to President Reagan at the April summit in Washington and resume the global strategy abandoned in 1985, namely, to put pressure on the United States to cut emissions.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITY ADVOCATED
CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITY ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like, once again, to express my grave concern about the precarious state of accommodation for Canada's Public Archives. I first raised this issue on June 6, 1986, during the debate on the Archives Act.
On December 8, last year, the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture tabled its report on the Public Archives. It found that the little space available for archival holdings and government records is spread over 14 locations in the National Capital Region. Moreover, this space does not meet the minimum atmospheric and environmental standards for the long-term preservation of our national heritage. The committee recommended the construction of a new Public Archives facility, located close to the National Library buildings.
The picture of burst pipes destroying our historical and cultural treasures, an embarrassment and threat to our sense of identity, was once again brought home during the Christmas recess when water severely damaged many priceless records in the Public Archives building itself.
This is the third time major damage has been caused to valuable collections of the library and archives since 1 first warned the House about this matter a year and a half ago.
I urge the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) to act immediately on the recommendations of the committee so that we can enter the next century without having lost the records of our past.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SCIENTIFIC CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE-TREATMENT OF MANITOBA UNIVERSITIES
ESTABLISHMENT OF SCIENTIFIC CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE-TREATMENT OF MANITOBA UNIVERSITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the National Conference on Technology and Innovation held just over a week ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the establishment of scientific centres of excellence.
Manitobans were shocked to read statements by unnamed senior civil servants that Manitoba universities would be frozen out of consideration for these institutes as long as Premier Pawley was the Premier of Manitoba.
Manitobans, from labour, business and government, and members of the Legislature in all Parties, protested when the CF-18 contract was awarded to Canadair because it was obvious that the bid submitted by Bristol Aerospace of Winnipeg came in at a lower price. Recent documents released as a result of inquiries by The Globe and Mail and Winnipeg Free Press indicate that not only was the Bristol bid lower, it was better technically.
People in Manitoba want fair treatment by the Government and they call on the Government, particularly Cabinet Ministers from Manitoba, to see that Manitoba is treated fairly.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT FUNDING-PRIME MINISTER'S ANNOUNCEMENT
GOVERNMENT FUNDING-PRIME MINISTER'S ANNOUNCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week some 200 of the nation's leaders with an interest in research and development participated in the National Conference on Technology and Innovation, chaired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
In his opening remarks the Prime Minister announced federal funding of $1.3 billion for new science and technology initiatives. Part of these funds is to create centres of excellence at a number of universities across Canada, and the creation of 2,500 undergraduate scholarships in science and engineering.

in his closing remarks the Prime Minister also announced a $10 million public awareness program to make Canadians more aware of the importance of research and development and its economic and social linkages.
Three themes were discussed in the forum workshops. They were revitalizing established industries; developing higher value products; fostering technology intensive firms.
Participants enthusiastically endorsed the new funding for the centres of excellence, the scholarships and public awareness program, but urged the Government to re-examine how tax incentives, advance rulings, and procurement could better assist research and technology intensive companies.
All agreed that the forum marked a new beginning and that Canada had turned a page in developing a knowledge intensive society.
Knowing your interest in this subject, Mr. Speaker, 1 am sure that you would have been proud to have been there.

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO INTRODUCE UNIFORMITY OF SENTENCING FOR CASES OF SIMILAR NATURE
OPPORTUNITY TO INTRODUCE UNIFORMITY OF SENTENCING FOR CASES OF SIMILAR NATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week in Ontario, we saw a case of sexual assault where justice has yet to be done. A woman suffered sexual assault with violence. She was beaten and suffered injuries.
Judge Vanini's decision in this case was shocking and irresponsible. He imposed a sentence of ninety days, to be served only on weekends because the defendant came from a good family. The judge decided the victim had suffered no serious psychological effects and that the defendant should stay in his family environment for the sake of his rehabilitation.
Mr. Speaker, I am amazed at the lack of concern and lack of sensitivity shown by Judge Vanini in this case. The judge seems to be punishing the victim and protecting the aggressor. The kind of stereotyping we see constantly in Canada's courts must stop.
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask all Canadian judges to seriously consider their attitude to women and what they suffer in cases of sexual assault, and I want to ask the Government to implement as soon as possible the recommendations of the Archambault report on sentence harmonization.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT'S PERFORMANCE
GOVERNMENT'S PERFORMANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until the middle of the 80s, Quebec's outlying regions were neglected by the previous Goverment as far as regional development was concerned. The northwestern part of Quebec, the Saguenay- Lac Saint-Jean area and the North Shore, as well as the Gaspe, the Lower St. Lawrence and the Magdalen Islands have always had special needs.
In 1984, the new Government, the team led by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), made these outlying areas one of its priorities for regional development.
In 1987, as part of the renewed federal policy for economic development, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, at the request of Cabinet, started a thorough evaluation of the economic requirements of these rural regions.
At Sept-Iles on December 22 last year, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. de Cotret) proposed a new regional development plan. Federal and provincial authorities have agreed to co-operate so that the plan can become effective as of April I, 1988.
Mr. Speaker, while the Opposition is still talking about these issues in Ottawa, we Conservative Members are doing something about them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the women of this country were shocked to hear that a man convicted of sexual assault in Sault Ste Marie received only a very light sentence.
A report published by the Metro Toronto Action Committee on Violence against Women and Children submits that judges in our judicial system tend to be more lenient with men of their own socio-economic class when these men are found guilty of sexual assault. This conclusion supports the arguments of many feminists who work with victims of sexual violence.
There are still so many stereotypes and myths that influence decisions made in criminal courts. The federal Government and the provinces must find a way to educate judges who preside over courts responsible for prosecuting sexual assailants.
It is imperative that Canadian women have access to a truly impartial judicial system. Otherwise, women who have been assaulted will be victimized a second time by the sentences handed out to the men responsible for these crimes.

subtopic: IMPOSITION OF LIFE SENTENCES FOR MURDERERS URGED
IMPOSITION OF LIFE SENTENCES FOR MURDERERS URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise in this House today with sadness in my heart and deep, sincere sympathy for the friends and relatives of the three innocent people brutally murdered in Chilliwack, British Columbia. An alleged repeat murderer not only murdered these three but also murdered the sister of one of my constituents in 1971.
It was just last year that some Members of this House voted against the reinstatement of capital punishment. They did this in spite of the wishes of the majority of Canadians who wanted changes to deal with the inefficiencies in our present judicial system. One of the main arguments was the fear of prosecuting an innocent person. Well, Sir, since that vote was taken we have lost four innocent people at the hands of alleged repeat murderers.
My respect for this House dictates that I accept its decision. However, I feel it is incumbent on this House to deal immediately with the system that has proven ineffective in dealing with those who brutally murder innocent people. We cannot bring back those already lost, but we can prevent recurrences of this nature, and we must act now.
I believe we must develop a system that incarcerates murderers for their entire natural life. Failing that, this House should reconsider its position on capital punishment.

subtopic: GRAIN HANDLERS' STRIKE AT PRINCE RUPERT-BINDING ARBITRATION PROPOSED
GRAIN HANDLERS' STRIKE AT PRINCE RUPERT-BINDING ARBITRATION PROPOSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is time for the Government to act to get grain moving through the grain port at Prince Rupert in British Columbia. This strike, which has crippled a large percentage of western Canada's shipments of grain for export, is having a serious affect on western grain farmers.
Last Friday the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) called on the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) to meet with the two sides involved in the Prince Rupert grain terminal strike this weekend and to persuade them to accept binding arbitration. He said that the Minister should be ready to suggest the name of an arbitrator to the parties.
Prairie farmers continue to face severely depressed grain prices. Prices are the lowest since the Great Depression. The last thing farmers need is to have grain backed up for weeks on
end. It is estimated that the farmers have already lost over $50 million.
The Leader of the Official Opposition has said that the grain transportation system is backed up, that elevators are clogged, and that farmers cannot deliver their grain. In addition, the Canadian Wheat Board is losing sales and Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier of grain is suffering. Both sides in the dispute must recognize that in failing to agree to binding arbitration they run the risk of having it imposed on them through legislation.

subtopic: GRAIN HANDLERS' STRIKE AT PRINCE RUPERT-CALL FOR BACK-TO-WORK LEGISLATION
GRAIN HANDLERS' STRIKE AT PRINCE RUPERT-CALL FOR BACK-TO-WORK LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, have you ever been robbed? Once again thousands of western Canadian grain farmers have been robbed of valuable grain sales, robbed of much needed income because of 69 union members and four grain companies unable to settle a strike at the Prince Rupert exporting grain terminal.
Over the years strikes and lockouts of grain handlers, longshoremen, rail unions and inspectors have taken the very food from mouths of farmers and their families. When grain producers right across western Canada are suffering from drastically reduced commodity prices while the average salary of a grain handler at Prince Rupert approaches $40,000 when benefits are included, farmers have a right to be steaming hot mad.
I urge the Government to legislate grain handlers back to work immediately and, further, to declare all aspects of grain handling and transportation systems affecting Canada's grain exports an essential service in order that the interests of western grain farmers and all of Canada best be served.

subtopic: LACK OF AFFORDABLE ACCOMMODATION IN TORONTO AREA
LACK OF AFFORDABLE ACCOMMODATION IN TORONTO AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of all the many concerns and problems that my constituents discussed with me over the Christmas recess, the lack of affordable housing in the greater Metropolitan Toronto area was the one raised most frequently.
Whether it was a young person looking for an apartment in a market where the rental vacancy rate is only 0.1 per cent, or a couple trying to buy their first home in a market where even the most modest house costs over $200,000, or a senior citizen facing a substantial rent increase with no prospect of alternative accommodation, all had first-hand experience with the problem, and understandably all are looking to Governments for solutions and for leadership.
There are no instant solutions, but the Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation can help to provide leadership by making federally owned land in Metropolitan Toronto available for affordable housing projects. One of his own consultants estimated that 15,000 such housing units could be built on federally owned surplus land at Downsview Airport.
How about it, Mr. Minister?

Mr. Speaker, as the Official Opposition critic for Youth, I have a duty to criticize the irresponsible attitude taken by the Minister of State (Youth) (Mr. Charest) in his announcement last week on Challenge 88. This is also true in Quebec, where youth unemployment is around 13.7 per cent. There is no excuse for letting this Program stagnate.
What about the national youth strategy! More than two years ago, the Minister promised us this strategy, and since then: Nothing! Improvisation is the name of the game.
