subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion (Mr. Mulroney) that Bill-103, an Act to increase economic opportunity in Atlantic Canada, to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and to make consequential and related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have indicated that there are certain aspects of this legislation which improve upon the previous approach taken. That is to say, under one ministry will be all of the programs for regional development related to Atlantic Canada. I would expect there to be more sensitivity than we have come to expect from the Governments of Canada, whether they be under the current administration or previous Liberal ones, to the two programs as they affect Atlantic Canadians and Atlantic Canadian businesses.

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
In this regard I need only refer to the Atlantic Enterprise Program which was introduced by the present Government.
In February of this year the Government had to respond very quickly to the criticisms which were launched immediately against the program by business people in Atlantic Canada concerning its threshold requirements. Initially, the program provided for loan insurance and interest buy-downs for projects in excess of $250,000. This refers to the program which was announced in the 1986 Budget.
The immediate reaction from Atlantic business people was that that would not apply to very many projects for capital improvement and that it would not provide any major initiative for development of capital projects in the Atlantic region. Within a matter of months the Government was required to announce, through the then Minister of State for Small Businesses, that the thresholds would be lowered from $250,000 to $100,000 and that interest buy-downs would be lowered from $250,000 to $25,000. This was in keeping with the scale of many projects and businesses in the Atlantic region. That is only one small example of what we in the New Democratic Party see as insensitivity by the members of Cabinet and by the Government to the needs of Atlantic Canada and to the importance of regional development to Atlantic Canada.
These difficulties that Atlantic Canadians have in getting a response from the Government of Canada to their needs are not new. They existed under the Tories. They existed prior to that under Liberal administrations. During the first five years of the DREE program under the Liberal administration, from 1969 to 1974, the per capita spending in the Province of Newfoundland was $9 per year. That was the annual average expenditure for the first five year period of the program. In the last five year period the per capita expenditure was down to $7. In the next year, which was a year under the Tory administration, the per capita expenditure for industrial incentive grants was down to $3. So we experienced a decrease, not an increase, in expenditures for this type of program. This was a program which was absolutely necessary, not only in terms of the interests of Atlantic Canada but in terms of the interests of the whole of Canada.
As I indicated before lunch, regional imbalances are the major economic problem of Canada. Since August of this year we have heard in the House statements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and other Ministers bragging about their performance. Figures released by the OECD Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development show that Canada's economy as a whole has been very good compared to other OECD nations. Our unemployment rate has dropped to a five year low of 9.1 per cent in the past year. However, not all Canadians have shared the sustained growth that Canada has experienced over the last several years. In the industrial heartland of Canada, in southern Ontario and in parts of Quebec, we are back to pre-recession levels. However, in the western provinces and in Atlantic Canada such is not the case.
The underlying message in all of this is that economic growth in Canada, powerful as it may be, will not cure the widening imbalances between regions. We are developing a two-tier system wherein there are two types of Canada's, a Canada for the economic heartlands and one for the fringes of the country, including Atlantic Canada. That is not good enough. It is not good enough for Atlantic Canada. It is not good enough for Canada as a whole.
Not just Members of Parliament from Atlantic Canada ought to be concerned about this matter. They are not the only ones from whom we should hear speeches on this subject. Members of Parliament from wealthier ridings, from ridings which have sustained economic growth, ought also to be concerned about the importance of regional development and about correcting regional imbalances.
Mr. John Crow, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, is one of many Canadians who has expressed concerns about regional imbalances. He has said that these regional imbalances could eventually drag down the whole economy. That is but one reason to support regional development. It affects the whole economy of the country. A more important reason to support regional development is that the people of Atlantic Canada deserve to have the same opportunities as do other Canadians in terms of employment. They deserve a share of the wealth of this great country.
The same report that the Prime Minister was so happy to quote in August and September of this year, put out by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, flagged to all industrialized countries the starkness of regional disparities in Canada's growth rates as a major problem. The agency has been quoted as saying that while such differences are a common feature of the Canadian economic scene, their intensity was unusually pronounced last year. That is an indictment against this country's approach to regional development. It is an indictment against the lack of concern that central Governments, both Tory and Liberal, have had for the regional development of Atlantic Canada. We in the New Democratic Party wish to see that change. We wish to see a national commitment to reducing the unemployment rate in Atlantic Canada.
The Minister of Transport stated in the House today that, "We will wait for four or five years and see if it works. We are putting in $200 million a year for five years and we will wait for four or five years and see how it works. The success of this is in the hands of the board that we have appointed". Atlantic Canadians, it is all your problem now. We are turning it over to you. We have taken away $1 billion per year, we are giving you back $200 million. In four or five years we will come and see how it has worked.
Instead of that, there ought to be a five-year commitment from the Government, or from any Government of Canada, to reduce the disparity between Atlantic Canada and the national
January 18, 1988

economy by 20 per cent per year. That is the type of commitment we expect from a Government that is serious about reducing regional inequities in this country. Let us put into the legislation that that is the goal and the objective of the agency, and that the Government is committed to making moneys available on an annual basis to achieve those results. Have the agency make an annual report to Parliament on the progress that it has made. That would be a real commitment to the reduction of regional disparities. All Canadians would then know, without even thinking about it, that if the unemployment rate in Ontario was the same as it was in Newfoundland, that would require a national project and would be a matter of national concern. It is a matter of national concern now because it is Newfoundland, just as much as it would be if it were Ontario, Quebec, or any other province.
Atlantic Canadians deserve better from this country. They deserve a commitment from the Government of this country to reduce the regional disparities. We want targets in the legislation, and we want input on that board from sectors of the economy in Atlantic Canada other than the private sector. We need to have input from the co-operative sector. We need stronger commitment from labour, an involvement by regional development corporations and associations, and a stronger input from the voluntary sector and organized labour. These commitments are needed if this Government is to be seen as taking seriously any commitment to regional development.
There is a concern that there is a lack of political will to do what needs to be done about regional development. That is the cases. It is exists in this Government. I quoted what was stated by the former Minister of Public Works, a Minister from the Atlantic region, who stated that "this is the last kick at the can". The five year commitment of $200 million a year for all of Atlantic Canada is the last kick at the can. This is all we can do. After that there ain't no more. If that is all that this Government can do for the next five years for Atlantic Canada, it does not deserve to be the Government of this country, and Atlantic Canadians will not support it.
Prior to the Government's involvement in 1984, the Liberal Government had a chance for 15 years, with the exception of the brief interregnum of the Government of the Right Hon. Mr. Clark. During that 15 year period the commitment to regional development decreased; it did not increase. In fact, the former Liberal Party regional development critic, a Member from Nova Scotia, admitted that his Party lost the political will to stimulate economic growth in the last years of former Prime Minister Trudeau's Government. That is an admission that the political will and the commitment was lost.
Indeed, when the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was Prime Minister, one of his first acts was to remove any Minister responsible for regional development. At that time, for the first time in 20 years, there was no one at the Cabinet table who was responsible for regional development. There was not one person whose responsibility was to see that regional development was to take place in this country. That was the extent of the loss of political will of the former Liberal
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
administration which existed up until September, 1984. That was when it ended. Since 1984 this Government has shown how badly it treats regional development as an issue.
A very poignant way of expressing the concern of this Government's approach to regional development was expressed in The Ottawa Citizen in May, 1987. The article states:
The Conservative government's approach to regional development seems to
have one potentially fatal flaw: As in Charles Darwin's theory on survival of
the fittest, some parts of the country may never flourish.
That is what has happened with the Government. It has one approach, and that is, if you are fit you survive, and otherwise you die. By taking money away from regional development in Atlantic Canada it is hanging Atlantic Canada out to dry, and all Atlantic Canadians will be the losers.
The people of Canada will rely on the New Democratic Party to make a commitment to a national effort on regional development; a commitment to attempt seriously in a targeted, programmed way to reduce economic disparities in this country, in a reasoned, carefully planned staged manner over a short period of time, and make the commitment to provide the funds to make that possible.
This can be done by way of the tax system. We know that the tax system as it presently exists favours the large corporations over the small. The economic reality of Canadian corporate structure is that the larger you are the less taxes you pay as a percentage of your earned income. Obviously that favours survival of the fittest. The fittest are those who will have more money to spend and co-operate with the Government to become larger at the expense of smaller enterprises. These smaller enterprises exist in the regions of this country.
Over the last 25 years we have seen a decrease in spending in the Atlantic region for regional development. In the late 1960s when DREE was first started, one-half of its budget went to Atlantic Canada. In the last year of the Liberal's power this had fallen to 22 per cent. In 1983-84 the Liberals spent $30 million less in the Atlantic region than in 1975-76. The people of Atlantic Canada cannot look to the Liberals for an answer. They cannot look to the Government for an answer. They will have to look elsewhere, to the New Democratic Party for a commitment on regional development.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we have heard from several Members of Parliament from the Atlantic provinces on this very important measure. Like the previous speaker, they made some excellent points that are worthy of consideration. This also is an example of the high calibre of debate that we receive in this House from Members of Parliament from Atlantic Canada.
Since the establishment of DREE in 1969, substantial attention has been devoted to the problem of regional disparity as it manifests itself in the Atlantic region. In fact, the experiences of the federal Government in trying to meet the special needs of this region predate DREE. There were a wide variety of initiatives undertaken beginning in the late 1950s.

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
There have been a multitude of broad strategies and individual initiatives. One survey identifies nine major and significant policy shifts since 1963. In addition, there have been major studies of the successes and failures undertaken by Governments and by independent agencies and scholars. The late DREE published regional and provincial reports; a select committee of the Senate produced a very insightful document; the Macdonald Royal Commission, the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, and the Cape Breton Advisory Committee have all reported recently.
Given the time which has now elapsed since the first attempts to address the problem, and given the amount of information and analysis now available, it should be possible to arrive at coherent and effective new policies. It is now urgent that this be done.
Governments, and particularly the federal Government, now have a severely diminished capacity to redistribute wealth because of their deficits and their strained sources of revenue. We appear to have reached the point where corporations feel able to demand that provincial Governments compete with each other in offering extravagant concessions in order to obtain development. What all the reports tell us basically is that regional development policies have failed utterly to lessen disparities between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of the country. It is possible to argue, hypothetically, that in the absence of those policies the disparities would be even greater, but that thought provides very little comfort. The statistical demonstrations of this failure are legion.
We know that social policies and equalization payments have raised disposable incomes closer to the national average and allowed the Maritime provinces to sustain levels of health and educational services which would otherwise be impossible. These, in turn, generate local economic activity. Compensatory policies not only signal a commitment to the right of all individuals to basic standards of living and of services in all parts of the country, but they also signal a rejection of the idea of leaving the Atlantic region to the mercy of market forces, which could well have the effect of emptying it entirely. Direct government activity, such as military installations, also contributes to the standard of living. This is to the good, and so is decentralized administration and procurement in the region. It is one thing to raise disposable incomes, however, and another to increase the production of wealth and thus to lessen the dependency of the Atlantic region.
Efforts to stimulate economic development and diversification have not led to increases in earned incomes relative to the rest of the country, or lessened dependence on public sector spending in general, and federal spending and transfers in particular. Federal transfers to Governments and individuals in Atlantic Canada exceed revenues by $7 or $8 billion a year and account for 75 per cent of gross provincial product. That is a tragedy. This is true despite the achievement of specific
objectives related to the creation of economic infrastructure and the stimulation of designated growth centres.
It is alarming to note that the low pay-off received from economic incentives has been consistent across several administrative approaches and changes in the nature of the incentives offered. There are some positive lessons to be gleaned. One is that projects do not outlast the incentives if they never made economic sense in the first place. They do not change the reality which discouraged investment in the first place, and they turn out to be a terribly expensive and demoralizing form of make-work project. The best DREE investments, by contrast, were in the expansion or modernization of existing viable enterprises, usually small to middle-sized and locally owned or controlled. It would be tempting in a time of fiscal restraint, but simplistic, for the federal Government to say that grants, tax incentives et cetera have not worked and thus should be abandoned. It would be simplistic because there is no evidence that these policies themselves are the problem or are unnecessary to generate economic growth. The truth is that traditional policy supports are almost certainly necessary, but apparently have not been sufficient to turn the Atlantic economy around. We must, therefore, recognize the fundamental problems which incentives and subsidies did not fully address.
Atlantic Canadians have to contend with a small market for their products. Although particular interest groups may see themselves threatened by prospects of freer trade with the United States, regional representatives should in general welcome the possibility of new economic opportunities in an expanded market. They and the Government of Canada must quickly identify the possible advantages and plan to seize them.
It has often been observed that some of the traditional disadvantages of Maritime industry, notably geographic ones, should not discourage the development of high technology industries, not to mention industries for which the region may in fact be uniquely suited. For example, several marine-related industries have been mooted in recent years. We should, therefore, be asking why outside capital is not attracted to genuine economic opportunities, especially when they are sweetened by incentives. It should equally be asked why these opportunities are often ignored even by indigenous entrepreneurs. If we knew why the Atlantic provinces were not considered attractive places to invest and why corporations hesitate to transfer highly skilled people there, we might understand why infrastructure and special incentives have not been sufficient to attract and hold industrial activity outside of natural resource exploitation. This is a roundabout way of posing a highly delicate question. Do the Atlantic provinces have characteristics which positively discourage or prevent investment? Do they produce enough skillful and ambitious entrepreneurs and managers, develop enough scientific and technological expertise, train a sufficiently qualified and
January 18, 1988

disciplined workforce to be taken seriously by outside investors? Do we drive out the best and brightest of those we do manage to produce?
The subjects of education, manpower training, research, entrepreneurship and investment incentives are related and fundamental to a realistic analysis of economic disparity.
We must acknowledge the problem and begin to consider fundamental changes or no amount of compensatory spending and short-term incentives will alleviate the chronic dependency of Atlantic Canadians. Our ability to match brains with the rest of the industrialized world will ultimately determine whether we can achieve the goals of social justice and humanity which all of us want.
At the present time the economy of the Atlantic provinces appears to be going through a crisis of confidence. This crisis is both economic and psychological. It is thus imperative that the Government of Canada undertake a new initiative to expand and diversify the economic base of the Atlantic region. This new initiative by the federal Government must be strong and determined and, by its nature, must be seen to be strong and determined. It, too, must have its economic and psychological effects but they must be growth promoting and confidence building.
Since the creation of the Atlantic Development Board in 1962, substantial amounts have been spent by the Government of Canada to encourage economic development in the Atlantic provinces. Very little of this money, however, has gone to the private sector to encourage directly the expansion of employment in manufacturing. Most federal funds have gone to provincial Governments to expand the infrastructure or the social overhead capital of the region.
Any survey of federal spending for regional economic development in the Atlantic provinces over the last two decades will reveal that direct incentives to industry have been relatively small, indeed so small as to be most unlikely to have any significant impact on the process of economic development. The fact is that there has never been a determined and realistic effort by the Government of Canada to expand and diversify the industrial base of New Brunswick and the other Atlantic provinces. Industrial incentives in aggregate have been relatively weak, weak in relation to those available in central Canada and perhaps, more important, the will in Ottawa to promote industrial change in Atlantic Canada has been extremely weak.
Citizens of New Brunswick and other Atlantic provinces contrast the enormous efforts and expenditures made by the federal Government to expand the automobile and aircraft industries of central Canada with the puny and perfunctory efforts at industrial development east of the Quebec-New Brunswick border.
Industrial development can only succeed if there are strong incentives for industry and there is the will in Ottawa to assist in using these incentives to promote economic change.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Regional industrial development must also become an important and pervasive objective of all the key economic Departments of the federal Government and must be coordinated to maximize its impact. In the past, industrial development in the Atlantic region has only been of peripheral interest.
What is the Government's response? The Government's response is before us today in the Bill to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, ACOA, has been designed by the Government of Canada to ensure the creation of a more favourable environment for sustained regional economic growth within which the people of Atlantic Canada will share increasingly the opportunities for employment and earned income available to other Canadians. The agency's prime objective is to reduce economic disparity between Atlantic Canada and the remainder of Canada through action, co-ordination and advocacy. ACOA is responsible for federal business and industrial development programs in the region with particular emphasis on small and medium-sized operations.
Its principal function is to design and deliver such programs, working closely with provincial Government and the private sector, and not as a substitute for the activities of other federal Departments. It has a particular responsibility to foster new enterprises at the local level. It has a strong co-ordinating mandate over all the region, particularly in job creation, training and skills development, local investment promotion, technology infrastructure development and procurement.
One of ACOA's objectives will be to build up the research capability of universities and other post-secondary institutions in Atlantic Canada and to ensure that regional enterprise is fostered. It is responsible for bringing a regional perspective to bear on the design of national economic and social programs that affect Atlantic Canada.
The agency, with its particular emphasis on business development aspects of regional development, seeks to stimulate the entrepreneurial environment of the region to improve the competitiveness regionally, nationally and internationally with small and medium-sized Atlantic businesses and to encourage adjustment generally to changing local and broader economic and market circumstances. The agency, guided by the advice of its board, seeks innovative ways in which to maximize the use of new and existing resources.
The board's views on the design and execution of flexible new programs and on the adequacy and possible modification of existing programs are being sought. In particular, the board advises the agency on ways in which the agency can work competitively with its clientele in programs to enhance economic and industrial growth, on strategies for ensuring Atlantic interests are addressed in the treatment of national issues, on methods for planning and co-ordinating economic

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
development activities in Atlantic Canada, on possibilities for stimulating productivity improvements and technological innovation in the region, and on needs for improved information, program-delivery systems and analysis of barriers to Atlantic entrepreneurial activity.
The legislation will give the Atlantic-based agency the legal powers and clout needed to implement an innovative economic agenda aimed primarily at small and medium-sized entrepreneurs and based on the vision and creativity of the people of the region. The Bill before us gives far reaching authority to the agency including direct influence on the programs of other federal Departments inasmuch as these affect the economic climate in Atlantic Canada.
Not only are the organizational and administrative characteristics of the Government's new policy in establishing the agency unique, but what sets ACOA apart is also the flexibility of its approach to promoting and supporting entrepreneurship in Atlantic Canada. Greater employment and higher earned incomes are dependent upon assisting entrepreneurs to realize their objectives without the impediments of regional disparity. The agency will have unprecedented authority of its own to assist small and medium-sized businesses, the types of businesses that create the most jobs.
This legislation gives the people of Atlantic Canada their first real chance to design economic policies which affect them directly. Following the Prime Minister's June 1987 challenge to Atlantic Canadians to become architects of their own economic destiny, numerous business and community leaders have been participating in an ongoing consultation with the agency regarding what needs to be done in Atlantic Canada. This dialogue will add well-thought-out program substance to the legislative structure before us today. It will also help devise effective guidelines to gain maximum benefit from the $1.5 billion of new money set aside by the Government for new ACOA programs.
The new legislation will allow the ACOA Minister and the agency to have a great deal of flexibility regarding decisionmaking in the region. It will allow co-financing of regionally advantageous projects with other Departments and the establishment of designated areas of exceptional opportunities. It will harness federal programs to the common goal of increasing opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada.
This is a Bill for the future. It is a Bill which gives Atlantic Canadians direction over their economic future. It is a Bill which places decision-making in the region where it belongs. It is a Bill which gives small and medium-sized enterprises the tools they need to encourage economic growth and stability in the region. It is a Bill which adapts regional development programs to regional needs, not regions to the strictures of development programs. It is a Bill which will help create the environment needed for economic growth. It is a Bill which has the flexibility needed to encourage real growth and prosperity in the region.
I urge all Hon. Members to read this Bill carefully because I know that if they do, they will agree that this is a Bill for a future of growth and prosperity for Atlantic Canada. I will conclude by asking Hon. Members to act quickly on this Bill for the sake of the future of Atlantic Canada and Atlantic Canadians. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to participate in the debate today.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this Government took office in September of 1984, $1.5 billion per year has been removed from support for the Atlantic region. Under the provisions of this Bill and with the funding we understand will be available, the Atlantic region will get $200 million per year in each of the next five years. This will mean that even when this Bill is passed and the funding is allocated, the Atlantic regions will still receive substantially less in federal government assistance to develop the Atlantic region than it was receiving when the former Liberal Government was in power. I would ask the Hon. Member how he can square the brave words we have just heard him utter with the reality of what the Conservative Government has done.
Second, how can the Hon. Member and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) argue that the free trade deal will give the Atlantic region the ability to get involved in procurement in the United States when he knows and the Prime Minister should know that the determined needs of the American Government and large American corporations are very large? Even if Canadian companies can get into the market, something that is doubtful, the contracts would go to companies in Ontario and Quebec, companies which are much larger and could therefore bid much more successfully for those supposed American contracts.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his very in-depth and well researched question. I think he has posed two very vital and important questions. The Hon. Member spoke of reality, so I would like to give him some.
The Atlantic agency has been given responsibility for all regional development programs relating to the Atlantic region including the following: the Atlantic Enterprise Program, the Industrial Regional Development Program, Enterprise Cape Breton and the economic regional development agreements. Along with these programs came the money to administer the programs.
The present level of expenditures under these programs amounts to approximately $196 million. That is a considerable increase over the regional development expenditures in Atlantic Canada by the last Liberal Government. Average expenditures under IRDAs and GDAs by the Liberal Government in the last three years of its mandate, 1981 to 1984, amounted to $146 million. Average expenditures under IRDAs and GDAs by this Conservative Government in the last three years amounted to $198.5 million. That is an increase in expenditures of over 35 per cent.
January 18, 1988

The Prime Minister and all Atlantic Ministers were not satisfied with this increase in expenditures and have therefore committed to the Atlantic provinces an additional $1.05 billion over the next five years, an additional $200 million yearly for five years.
The Hon. Member asked a question relating to freer trade. I am very glad to hear a realistic interest in that subject now being undertaken by his colleagues.
Living in New Brunswick and reading American newspapers, I have observed that in the New England states, there is a very low unemployment rate. There are large advertisements appearing in The Bangor Daily News every day asking for employees. There are not enough people to fill the jobs.
We can learn a lesson by getting into that market. We can build on the excellent universities which exist in the area. We can use the New England states, our natural trading partners along the Atlantic seaboard, as a market for our goods to enable us to expand. One mill owner has indicated that he will be expanding to the tune of 200 more employees which, while not much to people from central Canada, means an awful lot to us in Atlantic Canada.
In addition, what do the Americans want from the maritime provinces? 1 think they would like access to our two deepwater ports, Halifax and Saint John. If the Hon. Member examines the configuration of the Atlantic shelf as it extends out on the seaboard, he will find it is relatively shallow, with two big exceptions. Halifax and Saint John stick out into the Atlantic like two hungry jaws facing the Persian Gulf, from whence come the largest ships in the world. One of the things we can sell the Americans is a transportation facility extended all along the Atlantic seaboard.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for those searching questions and for giving me an opportunity to address important subjects.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I caught the reference by the Hon. Member to the development of the universities of New Brunswick, institutions in which I have a special interest because of my family background in that province. I know of the traditionally great love for learning among the people of New Brunswick, and one of the things I have been waiting to hear about in the debate today is the extent to which the educational institutions and programs available to the people of New Brunswick will benefit from this new Atlantic development program.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as some Hon. Members may know, this is a subject that I consider very important. It was the subject of a Private Members' Motion which all Members of this House approved of and passed. That Bill is now before the Standing Committee on Secretary of State for extensive study.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
One of the lessons we learned from the New England states and their development is the necessity to build on the expertise in our universities. That is what they have done, and the spinoff benefits in new industry and research and development have been simply tremendous.
We in New Brunswick have developed a centre of excellence in the form of a forestry complex which has received assistance from all the Atlantic provinces, the federal Government, as well as other provincial Governments. It is developing new techniques and opening a window on research in the vital forest industry. It has blazed a path which I would like to see ACOA follow. I know that in that agency's mandate there is a directive to address that subject, and I am very pleased with that.
One of the things we might do, for example, is to look at the business administration school at the University of New Brunswick and work with it to develop an international marketing concept that could help the private sector in the Atlantic provinces to expand and to develop new markets and new opportunities for growth.
Another thing we can do in concert with our universities is to develop an innovation testing centre, a science mall, which will test new inventions and disseminate knowledge about them to people in the area so we can create more jobs.
Another area we can work together on in the field of education is training. That is a direct responsibility of ACOA. We could work with our universities in developing education, training new entrepreneurs and our workforce in order to help make Atlantic Canada a Mecca for entrepreneurs and highly-skilled people in order to take advantage of freer trade and the other opportunities which exist in our country.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague on putting a very succinct case for the Bill before the House today. speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will pick up on the last statement made by the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). He said that no one has a monopoly on compassion for the Atlantic area or on a wish to see the Atlantic area develop and advance, i think that is right. Governments of all stripes have been stymied over the years and the decades in trying to come up with something that will work.
In spite of all efforts by Governments over the years we are still behind in per capita income and the disparities still exist. What we have done until now certainly has not worked very well. I hope that this initiative works. 1 doubt very much that it is the last initiative. My own people in Newfoundland have been around for 400 years and I doubt very much that we will pack it in tomorrow. Whether or not this is the last gasp or the last kick at the can, 1 do hope it works.
However, I have very serious reservations and some questions that I want to raise about this particular deal. 1 do not want to get into a debate with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) on who has the best record in the Atlantic provinces. He tried to make the case this morning that what the Liberals did was all bad and inconsequential and that what the Tories have done since 1984 has been excellent and outstanding. I would let the people decide that. The fact that we returned three Liberal Members out of seven in the Province of Newfoundland during the Tory sweep is indicative that the people know what has been done for them and who has been doing it. I think our record stands up in retrospect.
However, I do not think that kind of debate gets us anywhere. We should be asking questions about this particular deal. First, with respect to the $1 billion, the Government is very good at moving money around. It is the old shell game. They take the money away and then give it back and announce that they are giving new money. They did the same thing with R and D last week. In his economic statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) reduced incentives for research and development, particularly for technological firms, then the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that the Government was going to give $1.3 billion to research and development in Canada. They take it away one year and give it back the next; it is the old shell game.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
We have not yet seen any new money out of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The money which has been coming through is from the old DRIE program. We will wait and see whether any new money comes through.
The Minister of Transport said this morning that they were looking for ideas. That is a silly proposition to put forward. There is no shortage of ideas in the Atlantic provinces as to what needs to be done. If he looks on his desk he will see a pile of proposals from the Province of Newfoundland alone on what economic initiatives can be funded. To say that we are doing this because we want ideas from the Atlantic provinces is an absolutely silly proposition.
The Minister of Transport then said that Atlantic Canadians will have to depend on themselves to pull themselves up by their bootstraps. Well, we must give them the wherewithal, the context, and the proper incentives if we expect them to do that.
The main problem I have is that there is no commitment here to infrastructure. The Member for York-Sunbury talked about initiatives which he thought should be taken. He referred to two deep water ports. There is no provision under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, in so far as I can see, to deal with such things as deep water ports. Indeed, there is no mandate for them to deal with infrastructure at all. It says that they will continue to administer the existing ERDA agreements, but there is certainly no commitment to money.
As a matter of fact, the Minister of Transport made it very clear when he spoke on first reading that this initiative was for business purposes. That is my main criticism of the initiative before us. It is all very well to talk about encouraging business opportunities in Atlantic Canada, but Atlantic Canada is weak in infrastructure. Until such time as you close the gap between the level of infrastructure in the Atlantic region and the level in the rest of Canada there will not be a level playing field and equal opportunity.
You can talk all you like about offering a man money to set up a new fish plant or to apply technology to his fish plant, but if he does not have a paved road over which he can truck fish to market in good quality what is the point of setting up that plant? The same applies if he does not have three-phase power or water and sewer in the community. These are matters which should be addressed but are not addressed in the measure presently before us. There is no provision here at all for infrastructure.
If there is a difference between the policies followed by the Liberal Party when in government and the policies followed by the present Government, this is the fundamental difference. We tried to respond to needs in terms of infrastructure. The Minister of Transport will know that we built roads. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) referred to the road up the northern peninsula this morning. That is one of the roads that was built under previous DREE agreements. The other road which was started was that from Plum Point in his riding to Englee and Roddickton in my riding, but it has not been finished. The

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
road from Main Brook to the new St. Anthony airport has not been finished either, and nor has the trans-Labrador Highway.
There is an agreement for the TransCanada Highway and something like $10 million a year for the construction of the trans-Labrador Highway, but there is no new highways agreement in Newfoundland for secondary roads. We have had such an agreement before and are lacking that now. There is no provision in the legislation presently before us for carrying on with that kind of work.
1 submit that that kind of work is very important. We have to build those roads and water and sewer systems. We have to put in place the necessary infrastructure, particularly in small rural communities, if there is going to be equal opportunity for people to compete in the future. Indeed, I think we should turn the clock right back to the beginning and take a good look at the Atlantic Development Board, the original vehicle to address regional disparity.
In the report which Mr. Savoie made to the Government he recommended the same sort of things. I want to read from a story in Atlantic Insight in which they talk about a return to grass roots. They quote Mr. Savoie who was raised in Kent County in New Brunswick.
He says that a return to a more grass-roots, self-sustaining approach would be the better alternative. The article goes on:
Savoie used the old Atlantic Development Board (ADB) as a model for his new federal agency. Created in the early 1960's-
-created by a Conservative Government:
-the ADB was given six years to spend $150 million to improve the infrastructure of the region. During this period the area's highways were paved, hydro plants were built and much needed information on the Atlantic economy was collected-
The article goes on to say:
The board's last president, Ian MacKeigan, the 72-year-old former Chief Justice of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court, remains convinced that the ADB, with its local board of directors and less ambitious mandate, was a very better approach to regional development-
I suggest that this is true. All over Atlantic Canada one can see evidence of projects that were put in place by the Atlantic Development Board and which cannot be put in place by the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. It just cannot be done because it does not have the mandate and has no money to do it.
If we are going to make changes, I suggest we go back to the beginning and model the agencies on the Atlantic Development Board, to give it the flexibility and the money to invest not simply in business ventures but in infrastructure as well.
The Minister of Transport also said this morning that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be an advocate here in Ottawa. That suggests one of two things: Either there is no advocate, or the one that exists is not satisfactory.
I resent that as a Member of Parliament. As a matter of fact, one could probaby make the case that this infringes on the rights of Members of Parliament. We are elected as advocates. People vote for Members of Parliament to come here and be their advocate, yet the Government is telling us that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be an advocate. 1 resent that. Either the advocates are not there on the other side of the House or they are not doing their job. 1 think it is silly to talk about an agency being an advocate for an area.
There will be no benefit from being an advocate with other Departments because this legislation gives no guarantee that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will have any clout over other federal government Departments. It must be able to influence other Departments, particularly the Department of Transport and the Department of Finance. There is no indication that it will have any influence over those main line agencies.
While we need many new agreements, the one about which I feel most strongly is the renewal of the Labrador sub agreement. We were able to establish under that agreement much needed fisheries infrastructure on the Labrador Coast. We were able to build roads, put in water and sewer systems and were able to build nursing stations. That agreement has expired and there is no money to carry on that work. I would like to see that agreement renewed, but there is no provision for it in this legislation.
The whole issue of free trade has been mentioned. I think it is important to mention free trade in this context as well. I have seen no evidence that the Atlantic provinces will have any great advantage from free trade. As a matter of fact, no economist or other authority has shown me that there will be an advantage for the Atlantic provinces under free trade. I believe present disparities will be entrenched with the free trade agreement. If that is so, 1 think it is important that special provisions be made for the Atlantic area that would give us the necessary advantage.
The main problem I see with the free trade agreement is the provisions for energy. One of the fundamental economic measures one must take in Newfoundland in order to advance economically is the development of the hydro potential. In Labrador there is something like 10,000 megawatts of electricity. Yet that water is flowing to the sea every day untapped.
When the Premier of Newfoundland gave his support to the free trade deal, he evidently had some sort of commitment from the Prime Minister that he would get involved with the Government of Newfoundland and the Government of Quebec in advancing hydro development in Labrador. Yet Premier Bourassa announced recently a long-term, $1 billion agreement with the United States for the next 15 years with no new sources of energy, no development of the Lower Churchill. I do not know what commitment was given to the Premier of Newfoundland by the Prime Minister but there is no evidence
January 18, 1988

that any work is going ahead to advance the development of that hydro potential.
It will be even more difficult because of two requirements under the free trade agreement. One is the requirement to sign a long-term agreement with the Americans, assuring them of a continuing supply of energy over a long term period. The second requirement, which is even worse, is that we must guarantee the Americans no differentiation in price. In other words, we must sell to the Americans at the same price as we sell in Canada. Until now we had the flexibility of offering a made-in-Canada price to industrialists and entrepreneurs who want to set up in this country. That will no longer be possible.
I suggest that the free trade agreement itself, in this particular aspect, limits industrial and economic development in the future.
The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency also vaguely refers to training and development. It states that one of the mandates was procurement, training and skills development, job creation, technology, infrastructure development.
I hope the record of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be better in training and skills development than the record of the Government of Canada thus far. The record of the Government thus far has been to cut back on moneys available to young people for training and job creation. For example, there was the announcement during the Christmas recess that Challenge 88 will be kept at the same level it has been for the past two years. On the one hand, the Government talks about training and skills development yet, on the other, cuts back on existing funds. It has cut back on Established Programs Financing. The Minister of Finance announced that instead of proceeding with a 7 per cent increase over the next five years, he would only proceed with a 5 per cent increase, which means that the Province of Newfoundland will lose $181 milllion over the next five years for post-secondary education.
That is the record of the Government, yet we are told that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will become involved in training and skills development. There is no more important area with which it can become involved. It should begin with the problem of illiteracy, which is the greatest sore on the body politic. When we consider the level of illiteracy in this country, it begins with a rate of some 17 per cent in British Columbia, 20 per cent in Central Canada, and reaches a figure of 42 per cent in Newfoundland. While the program should begin by dealing with illiteracy, the reaction of the Government has been to throw $1 million nationally at the problem. Such an amount is peanuts, and virtually an insult.
How can we believe the Government is serious when it cuts back on Challenge 88, on Established Programs Financing and gives token lip service to a problem like illiteracy? While 1 hope the Government will take some brave initiatives for training and skills development, that has certainly not been its record so far.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
I hope this policy succeeds because what Parties on both sides of the House have done so far has not been as effective as it should have been. Otherwise the disparities would be erased and the gap closed. I hope this works, but I have very serious doubts as does everyone else. A survey of the Atlantic provinces Chamber of Commerce conducted in October found that only 18 per cent of the Atlantic provinces Chamber of Commerce membership believed that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency had any chance of dealing with regional disparity. More than 25 per cent said the chances were poor and 48 per cent said the prospects for success were only fair. There is not a great deal of enthusiasm for this particular measure. In spite of that, I do hope it works.
I doubt very much, given the present mandate, the present policy and the present allotment of dollars, that we are going to see a brave new world in the Atlantic in the very near future.

I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) a question but before 1 do so I would like to preface it with a few remarks.
The Hon. Member, seems to believe, at least from the context of his speech, that the infrastructure, which previous Liberal administrations had tried unsuccessfully for a good number of years to put in place is the key to the success of regional development in Atlantic Canada. I would remind the Hon. Member that Atlantic Canada has first-class engineering firms. Its 13 universities and technical colleges have highly qualified researchers working in well-equipped facilities. There are high-tech firms, enterprises dealing in all the products of the new industrial revolution throughout the entire region. There are service industries and manufacturing firms the equal of none. These engineers, researchers, industrialists, manufacturers and businessmen are competitive. They are deserving and anxious for government contracts and export opportunities. These firms are the equal of none. They excel in every way. I would also remind the Hon. Member that one of the jobs of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is to ensure that federal Government decision-makers know that these enterprises exist and what they do and that national policies and programs reflect an awareness of these facts.
I would suggest that previous administrations have been deficient in doing so. The agency will also keep on top of what other federal Departments and agencies do and plan to do in order to ensure that those plans, if they have a bearing on Atlantic Canada, meet the aims of the agency. It will not take too long for other Departments to become aware that there is an advocate for Atlantic Canada, contrary to the remarks of the Hon. Member. That advocate is the federal Government, this federal Government. It will not be long before federal activity in Atlantic Canada is more unified and joint action by Departments and agencies commonplace.

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
A unique feature of this Bill reinforces the Minister's coordination activities. That is Clause 9. That part of the Bill states that when the Minister is satisfied that the implementation of a program or project authorized by any other Act would further the purpose of the agency, the Minister may conditionally or unconditionally undertake to transfer funds appropriated for the purpose of ACOA to supplement funds that the Minister responsible for the program or project has undertaken to expend. This unique co-financing provision means that the Minister for ACOA can transfer ACOA funds to another federal project or program if that will help ACOA meet its objectives.
That means that ACOA will not have to develop its own programs where there may be programs administered by another Department that will be doing the same job. It means that if there is a progam that would help ACOA foster economic growth in the region, but the program cannot be extended or fully used in Atlantic Canada because of a funding problem, ACOA can then add funds so the program can benefit Atlantic Canada.
The co-ordination and co-financing inherent in the Bill gives the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency the flexibility it must have to pursue its purpose of economic growth in the region.
The Hon. Member has suggested that infrastructure is the way. How does the Hon. Member square that with the fact that he was a member of the Cabinet of the Government during the period of time when infrastructure was being touted as the way for restructuring, refinancing, and making Atlantic Canada independent of the regional disparity that we see there today? That was the old Liberal approach. How does the Hon. Member square his speech of today with the fact that those programs obviously did not work? As my colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) pointed out, $200 billion later we see that those programs have not worked. The Hon. Member stands and says he hopes this new program of this Government will work. He said that on at least three different occasions. Does this mean-after he tells us how his speech squares with the old approach-that he will indeed support the program, that it is worthy of his support and worthy of the support of all Members of this House?

Mr. Speaker, as an Atlantic Canadian I would like to say how much I welcome this initiative and how much my constituents welcome it. In many ways we are two years ahead of the Atlantic region in most of my riding because we have the Enterprise Cape Breton Board, which is a system that parallels what is proposed in the Bill before the House today. We have an autonomous organization with tremendous flexibility and local control.
By way of disagreement with the Hon. Member from Newfoundland I would say that there is nothing in this Bill which precludes agreements dealing with infrastructure. In fact, when the Minister who spoke first today addressed the question, he said only that the $1 billion would not be some kind of slush fund to administer infrastructure programs. He made it clear that the money was earmarked for business to achieve productive employment for Atlantic Canadians. He also made it clear that infrastructure type programs were still possible under agreements with the provinces. He was referring here to ERDA-type agreements. The Bill is very clear in giving to ACOA total flexibility to introduce new programs and to bring forward initiatives that are deemed to be in the economic development interests of Atlantic Canada.
In closing my comments I would like to say that this is not something that is totally new. We do not need to reach into the clouds to speculate about what all this means. We have a precedent in Atlantic Canada. It is called Enterprise Cape Breton. It is an enterprise which was brought forward to reflect the philosophical direction of our Government. It is an enterprise which has been very successful. In fact, it has been so successful that in the last 12 months the unemployment rate in Cape Breton has dropped from the 21 per cent range down to the 15 per cent range. Success speaks for itself. The principles that have been embodied in this Bill are the principles that are working for the people of my riding.

I want to comment on these jobs that have been created. The bulk of them have been created within a 60-mile radius of Metropolitan Toronto. In my region the latest unemployment figures show an unemployment rate of 13.3 per cent. In Newfoundland the rate is still at 18 per cent. Throughout the Atlantic region the rates are at very high, unconscionable levels. That is after three years of having a Tory Government in office based on a program of jobs, jobs, jobs. Those regions are still suffering regional disparities.
In its report of the week of August 22 the Economic Council of Canada comments on the, "starkness of regional disparities" in Canada's growth rates as a major problem.
As I stated, we drafted a report entitled Canada Unlimited, which is a compendium of very positive proposals with respect to building up the economies of areas like the Atlantic, northeastern Ontario, northern British Columbia, and the northern Prairies. We presented that to the Government. To date there has not been one move to implement any of those positive suggestions.
What we have here before us is Bill C-103 which is the Government's response. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) calls this response his "last kick at the can". He tells the people of the Atlantic that this is their "last kick at the can". 1 think that he should be put in the can. Then all of us can go and have a kick at it.
Can you believe, Mr. Speaker, the depths of hopelessness? This Minister is saying if ACOA does not work, that is it. The Government is giving up. That is what the Minister of Public Works has stated. He states that this may be the "last kick at the can" as far as development programs for the region are concerned. He then turns around and tells the people in the
Atlantic region that they will be responsible for this program. The Government states that the people of the Atlantic will be responsible for the program. Of course, the suggestion is that if the program fails it is not the Government's fault. It is the blame-the-victim syndrome again. It is the fault of the Atlantic people not the fault of the federal Tory Government.
Earlier today we talked about the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) before he became Prime Minister running in the by-election in Central Nova in the Atlantic region. He no sooner got that seat than they never saw him again. He cut and run. It is only when he was embarrassed while appearing at the 300 Club in Halifax that he put his face back in Central Nova, after he had deserted the Atlantic region. I want to tell the Tories that this is their last kick at the can. If they have the courage to call an election shortly, they will find themselves kicked right out of the can.
In principle we have no problem with decentralization. But when we look at what is proposed for this program, we cannot agree with the funding. In effect when listening to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) this morning, and when listening to the Government and the Prime Minister, one would think that the Government is putting up $1.05 billion over five years and that this is a great pile of new money that it is putting into the Atlantic region. In fact, it is the old shell game.
Since 1984 when the Conservatives took power, they have cut approximately $1.5 billion annually from the various federal government spending programs in the Atlantic region. Can we remember those heady days when they were all gung-ho on cutting deficits? They had old Erik Nielsen-velcro lips-who proposed the program called the Nielsen report which drastically cut programs in the Atlantic region. Every day in the House we were screaming at the Government about the cut-backs. Well, they came to $1.5 billion annually. What the Government has removed, it is now telling us it will compensate the Atlantic region by putting $200 million a year back in over five years to come to $1.05 billion. That is a laugh.
In this Bill we also have the principle of decentralization. The Government states that it will decentralize. It is not going to be like the old DREE programs where Don Jamieson was the Minister here and all the bureaucrats in Ottawa decided which programs were going to go in the Atlantic region, in northern Ontario, and in other regions of the country. They stated that that will not be done any more. It was the old sleight of hand. They stated that they were decentralizing and setting up this agency with 19 members on the board. I will come to those specifics about the 19 in a moment. But there will be 19 members on the board. Not all of them have been appointed as yet. The headquarters will be in Moncton. There will be sub-head offices in each of the Atlantic provinces. There will be 300 bureaucrats.
The question you might want to ask, Mr. Speaker, is that not decentralization? I know that is what you are thinking, Mr. Speaker. I can see by the look that that is the thought you

have in your mind. As much as 1 know that you would like to support that principle of decentralization, Mr. Speaker, it is not decentralization. When you strip away all of the verbiage and the rhetoric, the decisions are still going to be made here in Ottawa, and of all places, in the other place.
In the discussions on Bill C-22 the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) stated that it was an undemocratic place. They were not elected over there. Senator Lowell Murray will be the chief honcho for this operation. In fact, that is set out very clearly in Clauses 5, 6, 7, 20, and 21. The powers rest with the Minister who is a Senator and who is not elected. The powers rest over there. He will then appoint a chief operations officer, a chap by the name of McPhail. His duties are the duties of a Deputy Minister. The bureaucracy rests here. The Minister has the authority to approve or not approve any project. The Minister calls the shots, so the shots will still be here in Ottawa. That is not decentralization at all. In fact, Clause 11 reveals the close ties between the President and the Minister. It states:
(2) The President is the chief executive officer of the Agency and, under the direction of the Minister, has control and supervision over the work, officers and employees of the Agency.
So what is the purpose of the board? The question then is, what does the board do? The board has no power. It is a roaring rabbit, a toothless tiger. That is what it is. It is the old program all dressed in drag. It is the old DREE without the bucks, or with money that was taken from the Atlantic in the first place.
What does the board, the agency, those 19 Tories do? They assist and advise-"assist" is the word. In the legislation it says that the board's purpose is to assist. We do not know what assist means. Does it mean assisting them with their fund raising for the Tory Party? So far most of them who have been appointed are baghacks and flicks for the Tory Party. That is not our view of decentralization. Decentralization for us means that the decision making rests there. If there is a board, then the board is accountable and it is accountable to the regions. Decisions have to be made in the regions, not here in Ottawa, as this legislation allows.
We also have a concern about commitment to regional development. As we see it, in spite of what the Government has said about its commitment to regional development, that commitment over the years has declined. In 1984-85, explicitly, regional development for all of the Atlantic region was in the order of $230 million. By the way, that is around 15 per cent of what the UI pay-out is in the Atlantic. Expenditures on DRIE's industrial incentive programs have decreased in real terms from $9 a person in

The other thing concerning us about the way this agency has developed, and we have noticed it in the same way with the Northern Ontario Development Corporation, FEDNOR for short, is the insidious implementation of the patronage principle. SUGGESTED PARTICIPATION Op WORKERS IN PAID EDUCATIONAL LEAVE PROGRAMS

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing a measure enabling workers to participate voluntarily in paid educational leave programs, in order to foster their vocational training and their adaptability to the requirements of the labour market, thus reducing the impact of the devaluation of their skills and, by extension, overall unemployment, and encouraging economic growth and the security of Canadian workers.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I would like to put forward the rather simple proposition that Canada's continued prosperity depends on the training of our workers. Further, it is clear that we are not doing nearly enough. It is perhaps trite to say but nevertheless I think evident, that it is time for action and leadership by the Parliament of this country and by its Government. It is time to do something to remedy the situation and to deal with a problem which is clearly evident, the problem that Canada does not do nearly enough training as compared to our competitors in the global market-place.
Furthermore, there ate a number of well thought out policies which can be implemented immediately. My motion today addresses one such policy, that of paid educational leave, which was studied in 1983 by a task force set up by the then Minister of Employment and Immigration. Such a policy has been implemented successfully in a number of European countries and in Japan. The concept was endorsed recently by the Economic Council of Canada in its 1987 report entitled Innovation and Jobs in Canada.
Last week, I attended the National Conference on Technology and Innovation in Canada. I can report to Members of the House that the question of training of the workforce was a matter which received prominent attention in the workshops and the plenary sessions. Mr. David Culver, the Chairman of Alcan, reminded us in his keynote address of the social and cultural fall-out of modernization. He said that there is almost always a loss of jobs when a company modernizes itself or when a country goes through such a process. He stated that there is a clear role for Government to ensure that there is timely retraining for those who are displaced.
I would like to dwell briefly on some comparisons with other countries. Japan is perhaps the best example of dedication to training or retraining. We have now become familiar with the idea that the Japanese bank on employees' loyalty to companies to make it worth-while to train and retrain. They are not afraid that their employees will leave them for better jobs after investing considerable amounts in their training.
For every one hour of training received by a North American worker, the average Japanese worker receives approximately 100 hours of training. Indeed, similar figures were referred to by John Evans, the President of Allelix, at the conference in Toronto last week. He said that employees in the computer industry in Canada receive two hours of training for every 100 to 200 hours received in Japan.
The Nissan company recently opened a plant in Smyrna, Tennessee, I believe. It is quite remarkable but that company spent $63 million to train workers before the plant door was even opened and before even one car came off the production line.
In West Germany, the situation is similar. That country has a number of well developed vocational training programs which are largely credited as being the foundation of West Germany's economic success. These programs are administered co-operatively by the federal and provincial or state Governments. They use what is known as the dual system in which there is a mix of on-the-job and off-the-job training.
In 1984 and 1985, Siemens, a large manufacturing firm, took on some 10,000 apprentices. It spent an equivalent of some $250 million on these apprentices in addition to the $300 million it spends on training its ongoing personnel. This one company maintains a staff of 500 full-time teachers and 3,000 part-time teachers.
Of course, West German firms responded to the worldwide recession of 1982 by increasing, not decreasing, the number of trainees taken on by some 46,000 persons. In West Germany, there were 677,000 apprentices in West Germany. In 1984, one year later, this figure had risen to 706,000.
While the training figures of Japan and West Germany are increasing, Canada's are decreasing. In 1983-84, participants in what was known as the National Training Program which was run by the Department of Employment and Immigration totalled some 277,000 persons. This fell to approximately

206.000	in 1985-86. The National Training Program was absorbed by the Canadian Jobs Strategy in September of 1985 and became Skill Shortages and Skill Investments. In 1986-87, these two programs registered a total of 88,700 participants and it is estimated that in this fiscal year, 1987-88, only
117.000 participants will be involved in those two programs, Skill Shortages and Skill Investments. Again, that is 117,000 as compared to some 277,000 only three or four years ago, not even half the number.

Mr. Speaker, a policy of paid educational leave would make it possible for working men and women to earn days of leave for the purpose of education or professional training. The possibility of such a program was adressed in 1983 by the Skill Development Leave Task Force. It was one of several programs considered by this task force. Its members emphasized the fact that educational leave would offer equal opportunities for all only if it were biased in favor of the academically poor.
The experience in other countries has demonstrated that adult education is often the privileged domain of those men and women who have already benefited from a high school or even university education. An increased participation by blue collar workers and members of all classes of our society would depend on the implementation of special programs directed at minority groups or team workers in order to discourage the formation of a class of workers who are both unskilled and underpaid.
The National Advisory Panel which followed the task force study suggested that such leave could be earned at a rate of one day for every thirty days of work. In this case, Mr. Speaker, each working man and woman could gain as much as eight days of educational leave per year of work. The National Advisory Panel recommended then to the federal and provincial governments to adopt immediately legislative measures to implement such programs.
The Economic Council of Canada, in its 1987 research report entitled Innovation and Jobs in Canada, endorsed the concept of paid educational leave. It said:
We would like to focus attention once again on the feasibility of implementing a paid educational leave policy in Canada.
With respect to funding, the national advisory panel, in 1984, again recommended a 1 per cent personal income surtax and a 3 per cent corporate income surtax in order to raise the approximately $500 million necessary to operate such a program. One reason for calling for such a surtax was to encourage the participation of all workers. As I said earlier in my remarks, it is mainly the well-educated who benefit from various forms of continuing education and adult education in Canada. As I also said, special measures are required, such as including workplace delegates to encourage all workers to participate in the program.

The national advisory panel, in considering its funding mechanism, thought that by paying for such a program through a personal income surtax all workers would be prompted to involve themselves in retraining because they would be paying for it. They would see this on their tax bill every year and therefore would be encouraged to get a benefit from some of their tax dollars and get involved in some form of ongoing educational program.
At the time that recommendation was made, I had certain concerns about the funding mechanism. As you will recall, in 1984 we were perhaps 18 months into a recovery from the 1982 recession. The balance sheets of Canadian companies had been hit hard. I felt that a corporate income surtax would be hard to contemplate. No one likes to contemplate the idea of increased personal income taxes either. At the time I felt that the federal Government ought to share the cost of establishing a universal paid educational leave program on a, for example, fifty-fifty basis. I felt that federal funds could be made available through reallocation of and savings in existing programs, including industrial support programs.
We are far too ready to put money into bricks and mortar and new machinery but reluctant to invest in our workforce. To this day 1 feel that there is room within the various industrial support programs for the retraining of workers, and my views on the funding mechanism have not changed over the course of the past couple of years. We have seen very stiff increases in personal income taxes imposed by the Conservative Government since the 1984 election and I feel that an additional income tax is probably out of the question in the minds of most Canadians. Therefore the federal Government ought to share the cost of establishing such a program, as 1 said, on a fifty-fifty basis. The part not paid by the Government would be paid by the employer and employee, with the amount subject to negotiation between the parties.
You will see that my motion is presented in the way of a recommendation. It says:
Thai, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the
advisability of introducing a measure enabling workers to participate
voluntarily in paid educational leave programs-
It is framed in that fashion because, as you know, Private Members cannot put forward Bills which entail the expenditure of money. That is a government prerogative and requires Royal Assent. If we did not have this restriction you would see a Private Members' Bill which would propose actual legislation to implement such a program. It would probably contain recommendations for funding in the first year of the program and perhaps in several subsequent years.
However, as 1 said, because Private Members cannot put forward a Bill in that fashion, I have framed this motion in a very innocuous fashion. All I am asking the Government to do is to consider the advisability of such a program. I would like to suggest to my colleagues that such an innocent proposal is worthy of their support.

Some 250 people from across Canada studied the matter and a national advisory panel recommended that legislation be introduced to put the idea into practice. The Economic Council of Canada endorsed the concept in 1987, and there is widespread recognition that we are not doing nearly enough to retrain our workforce or, more correctly, permit it to engage in various forms of ongoing training.
